titulo.texto: The Xantolo Altar Arch / Festival of the Souls

frase_gancho.texto: An arch of yellow flowers so that souls can find their way home.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the festival of the dead, we move on to the white clothing of the Totonac people. Look for a white cotton suit, with a red kerchief tied around the neck and a palm hat.

guion_corto.texto: This is a reconstruction of a Xantolo altar, the festival of the dead in the Huasteca, in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Veracruz. The most striking feature is the great arch made of flexible rods and covered with intensely yellow marigold flowers and green foliage. It is thought to be the door through which souls return to visit their families. Beneath the arch, the table is set with food: large tamales, bread, chocolate, fruit and candles, along with copal that perfumes the air. Everything is prepared with care, because the dead return, and the living welcome them with what they loved most. Xantolo blends ancient beliefs with the Catholic calendar and lasts several days.

guion_largo.texto:
“Xantolo” comes from the word “santos,” meaning “saints.” It is the name given in the Huasteca to the festival of All Saints and All Souls' Day, which is celebrated in late October and early November. All over Mexico, offerings are placed for the dead, but each region has its own style. Here the style is an arch of flowers, a banquet and a great stir of people.

Let's begin with the arch. It is made of flexible rods, bent into the shape of a door, and covered with marigold flowers and green foliage. It is thought to be the threshold through which the dead return home. The flower has its own story: its Nahuatl name, cempoalxóchitl, is usually explained as “flower of twenty.” Its intense yellow color and strong scent, it is said, help souls find the way. You have already seen [Xochipilli](mna_s06_xochipilli), the “prince of flowers,” in the Mexica Hall; here, flowers remain a language shared with the gods and with the dead.

The table. Beneath the arch, the family places what the departed loved: tamales, chocolate, bread, fruit, and sometimes sugarcane liquor or coffee. In the Huasteca there is an enormous tamal, sometimes more than a meter long, called the zacahuil. It is not just a dish: it is a way of saying that the one who has gone remains part of the table. Copal, that perfumed smoke you saw in the [Otomí oratory](mna_s15_oratorio_familiar), helps invite the souls.

The road of the dead is ancient. In the Mexica world, the departed went to Mictlán, a long journey of several years, with the help of a dog, like the one you saw in the [Colima figures](mna_s10_perros_colima). Today those ideas blend with the Catholic calendar and with the annual visit of the souls. The festival falls on the dates of All Saints, but it seems older, and it is thought that in pre-Hispanic times it was celebrated at other times of the year.

In the Huasteca, Xantolo is not only the offering. There are troupes of masked dancers who travel through the villages with violin and guitar music. The costumed figures represent the dead and the living, and they move among laughter and mockery. It is a way of making peace with death, and of remembering that the festival belongs to the living as well.

Death here is not an ending, but a visit. The children arrive first, on the night of the thirty-first, and the adults come afterward. Each family cleans the house, prepares the food and waits. When the festival ends, the souls return to their world, and the family is left with the feeling of having been together again. Perhaps for that reason, the celebration, besides being sad, is deeply grateful.

There is one last fact. In the year two thousand eight, UNESCO recognized the indigenous festival dedicated to the dead in Mexico as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It is a recognition of a tradition that unites peoples as different as the Purépecha of Lake Pátzcuaro, the Huastec and the Nahua of the sierra. Each one sets out its own arch, flowers and food, but all celebrate the same thing: seeing one another again.

texto.People: Tének and Nahua Peoples of the Huasteca
texto.Region: Huasteca of San Luis Potosí, Veracruz and Hidalgo (Tempoal, Huejutla)
texto.Technique/Material: Otate rods, palmilla, cempasúchil, carved wax, copal, bread and wood
texto.Function: Ceremonial altar and sacred installation for the Xantolo festival (Day of the Dead)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Day of the Dead is a sad festival of mourning.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a visit: families welcome their dead with flowers, food and music. Sadness and joy are mixed together.
